---
title: "Methods"
---

Implementation notes for the choices that are hard to read from the code. The Methods
section of the manuscript is the authoritative description.

## Model

One XGBoost regressor per site, target `NEP_ZSCORE`, predictors `TA_ZSCORE`,
`SWIN_ZSCORE`, `VPD_ZSCORE`, `SWC_ZSCORE`. Settings are in `src/models.py`:

```python
tree_method='hist'
subsample=0.8
colsample_bytree=0.8
reg_lambda=1.0
reg_alpha=0.1
gamma=0.2
min_child_weight=5
early_stopping_rounds=100
```

The hyperparameter search (`TUNE_HYPERPARAMETERS = True`) covers `n_estimators` 2000 to
4000, `max_depth` 4 to 8 and `learning_rate` 0.01 to 0.1, 125 combinations per site.

## Flux targets

| Target | Source variable | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| `NEP_ZSCORE` | `NEE_VUT_50`, sign flipped | Measured, quality flag 0 only |
| `GPP_ZSCORE` | `GPP_NT_VUT_50` | Partitioning product |
| `RECO_ZSCORE` | `RECO_NT_VUT_50` | Partitioning product |
| `ET_ZSCORE` | derived from `LE_F_MDS` | Includes gap-filled values |

Median out-of-sample R2 across the 208 sites: NEP 0.64, GPP 0.67, RECO 0.58, ET 0.67.
RECO comes from a temperature response fitted to nighttime NEE and extrapolated into the
day, and GPP is RECO minus NEE, so part of any temperature signal in their attribution
belongs to the partitioning. The LE quality filter is disabled in `src/files.py`, because
the FLUXNET flag marks every LE record as gap-filled.

## Cross-validation

`random`, behind the published results, is a shuffled 5-fold split. `blocked` holds one
calendar year out at a time and skips sites with a single year. Over 206 sites the median
out-of-sample R2 falls from 0.64 to 0.54; the Stage 8 VPD contribution is unchanged
(-0.429 against -0.429) and the soil water contribution weakens from -0.085 to -0.064.

## Predictor sets

`FEATURE_SET` in script 31: `full`, `no_vpd`, `no_ta`. Dropping either variable lowers
the score at 205 of 208 sites (median R2 0.64, 0.60 and 0.61). Each variable takes over
part of the other's role when removed, so the attributions in the full model are
conditional on both being present. The `no_ta` run is carried through the aggregation:
the threshold from models that never saw temperature is 1.28 kPa [1.19, 1.37] against
1.26 kPa [1.16, 1.36], one row of Table 1. A model with TA and a different humidity
variable is not possible, because every humidity variable derivable from these data is a
function of TA and VPD.

## SHAP

`TreeExplainer` with `feature_perturbation="tree_path_dependent"`, which keeps the
observed joint distribution of TA and VPD. The result is a conditional attribution of the
fitted prediction among correlated predictors, not a separation of physiological causes.
SHAP values are out-of-sample: each fold explains only the 20 percent its model never
trained on.

## ALE

`PyALE.ale`, 100 grid points per predictor, one model per site fitted on 85 percent of
the records. These are separate fits from the cross-validated models behind the SHAP
values. ALE and SHAP interrogate models of the same form on the same data, so agreement
between them tests the interpretation method, not the physiology.

## Soil water layer {#soil-water-layer}

The published analysis uses `SWC_F_MDS_1`, the shallowest layer. With
`SWC_LAYER = "deepest"`, script 21 takes at each site the deepest layer that holds at
least 90 percent of the records of layer 1 within the peak months
(`src/common.py::deepest_swc_per_site`). The coverage floor keeps the sample the same
between the two runs; without it, 18 sites would have run on a much sparser layer.

Under this rule 128 of 208 sites move to a deeper layer (layers 2 to 9) and 80 stay on
layer 1, so a `deep-sm` run keeps all 208 sites and 80 of them are bit-identical to the
shallow run. `SITE_SUBSET = "deeper-only"` restricts both runs to the 128 sites that
moved, which is the matched pair. Depths in centimeters are not recoverable from the data
products.

Stage 8 ratio of the VPD to the soil water attribution: 5.03 shallow and 4.86 deep over
all 208 sites; 4.22 and 4.00 on the matched 128. Only 10 of 30 evergreen broadleaf sites
have a usable deeper layer.

## Stress stages

Nine record subsets defined on z-scores in `src/stages.py`, with cut-offs at 0.319
(middle 25 percent), 0.714 (next band) and 1.282 (outer 10 percent) of a standard normal.

| Stage | Condition |
|-------|-----------|
| 0 | all records |
| 1 | TA, VPD and SWC within the middle 25 percent |
| 2 | warm, soil moisture normal, VPD not extreme |
| 3 | warm, dry soil, VPD not extreme |
| 4 | hot, dry soil, VPD not extreme |
| 5 | hot, very dry soil, VPD not extreme |
| 6 | extremely hot, very dry soil, VPD not extreme |
| 7 | extremely hot, extremely dry soil, VPD not extreme |
| 8 | extremely hot, extremely dry soil, extremely dry air |

Standardization does not make the drivers Gaussian; script 87 measures the empirical
share of records below each cut-off (within six percentage points of the Gaussian share
at the median site, within two at the Stage 8 cut-offs). Shortwave radiation is not
constrained by the stages and rises from 0.34σ at Stage 1 to 0.65σ at Stage 8 (script
45). The sequence is not a factorial design. Three tests address that: the mirrored stage
order, the matched records and the factorial cells.

### Stage order

`mirror_1` to `mirror_8` in `src/stages.py` swap the roles of VPD and soil water: VPD
escalates through the stages and extreme soil dryness is added last. Stage 8 is the same
records in both orders. Script 88 compares them:

| Order | Second to last stage | Final stage | Cost of the last step |
|---|---|---|---|
| published, extreme VPD last | -0.07 | -0.36 | -0.29 |
| mirrored, extreme soil dryness last | -0.24 | -0.36 | -0.12 |

The mirrored Stage 7 holds about twenty times more records than the published one,
because capping soil dryness restricts less than capping VPD.

### Record matching

Within the cut-offs, Stage 8 records are hotter, drier and brighter than Stage 7
records. Script 89 pairs every Stage 8 record of a site with the closest Stage 7 record
of the same site, with replacement, within 0.5σ in TA, SWC and SWIN; the strict variant
also requires the same calendar month and the hour of day within one hour. Script 59
writes the summary as part b of Supplementary Table 5.

| | Strict | Covariates only | Unmatched, same sites |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sites with pairs, of 145 with both stages | 140 | 144 | 145 |
| Stage 8 records matched | 60 % | 81 % | |
| Difference after matching, TA, SWC, SWIN, VPD (σ) | +0.15, -0.02, +0.04, +0.98 | +0.14, -0.01, +0.01, +1.09 | |
| Net effect difference, median site (σ) | -0.26 | -0.31 | -0.27 (mean) |
| Sites with a negative net difference | 91 % | 94 % | 83 % |
| VPD contribution difference, median site (σ) | -0.21 | -0.23 | |
| TA, SWC, SWIN contribution differences (σ) | -0.03, 0.00, -0.02 | -0.02, 0.00, -0.02 | |

Shortwave radiation is balanced after matching. The residual TA imbalance of 0.15σ
contributes 0.03σ through the TA attribution.

### Factorial cells

`FACTORIAL_CELLS` in `src/stages.py` splits the records into four soil water classes by
four VPD classes at the same cut-offs as the stages, with TA unconstrained. Class 0 is
the middle 25 percent, and classes 1 to 3 step toward stress at 0.714 and 1.282, down for
soil water and up for VPD. Records with wet soil or low VPD fall in no cell. Script 44
with `STAGE_SEQUENCE = "factorial"` aggregates the sixteen cells into its own
`factorial-cells/` folder. Script 69 writes Supplementary Table 10: per cell the sites,
the records and the SM, VPD and net effects as the mean of the site means, with the
interquartile range across sites.

With the other driver in its central range, the VPD effect at extreme VPD (-0.40σ) is
about five times the SM effect at extreme SM (-0.08σ). Each effect is nearly the same in
every class of the other driver: -0.40σ at extreme VPD in all four soil water classes and
-0.08σ at extreme soil water in all four VPD classes.

### Stage 8 by site

Part a of Supplementary Table 5 (script 59) raises a minimum number of Stage 8 records
per site from 1 to 100 and reports the sites that remain, their mean VPD and SM effects
and the ratio of the two with a bootstrap interval over sites. Two rows pair the effects
at each site, each the mean over the Stage 8 records of that site: the share of sites at
which the VPD effect is more negative than the SM effect, and the median across sites of
the VPD minus SM effect. Without a minimum, the VPD effect is the more negative at 146 of
160 sites (91 percent), with a median difference of -0.37σ.

## Aggregation across sites

Every site contributes one curve or one binned grid with equal weight. Aggregated bins
are kept where at least half the sites have data. Spread across sites uses the law of
total variance (`src/stages.py`); bars in the stage figures show the standard error of
the site means.

## Threshold definition

The threshold is the highest VPD at which the fitted VPD contribution crosses from
positive to negative. From SHAP (script 54): a fourth-order polynomial fitted to the
cross-site median per bin of the TA by VPD grid, one point per bin. From ALE (script 46):
a fourth-order polynomial fitted to each site curve, then the mean of the per-site zero
crossings with a t-based 95 percent interval; the crossing of the pooled curve (0.107σ
against 0.181σ) is written beside it. Both are zero crossings of a model attribution.

Script 81 separates the peak of the VPD contribution (0.47 kPa), its zero crossing
(1.26 kPa) and its steepest decline (1.50 kPa), and flags points within 2 percent of the
range edge. The minimum is flagged in every group, since the curve is still falling where
the data end.

### Conversion to kPa

Per site, `VPD_kPa = (site mean VPD + z * site SD) / 10`, over the records the models
saw, then averaged across sites with equal weight; a forest type value is the mean over
its sites, and interval bounds go through the same conversion. CD-Ygb stores VPD in Pa
and is divided by 100 first; unconverted it moves the all-sites threshold from 1.26 to
2.19 kPa.

### Estimator sensitivity

Script 47 re-estimates the threshold under 23 settings: polynomial degrees 2 to 6,
LOWESS at five bandwidths, smoothing splines over two orders of magnitude, four bin widths
and five fitting ranges. All fall between 1.23 and 1.29 kPa; the published fit sits at
the median. LOWESS runs lowest, 0.155 to 0.174σ.

### Leave-one-site-out

Script 47 drops each site in turn and refits: 1.253 to 1.268 kPa, median 1.264, largest
shift 0.010 kPa (US-CMW). Table 1 reports the range, since the 208 values share 207 sites
each and are not independent.

### Site VPD range

A site with a narrow VPD range reaches +3σ at a modest absolute VPD. No site stays below
1.25 kPa (lowest site maximum 1.69 kPa), so script 82 splits the sites into quartiles of
their maximum VPD:

| Quartile | n | Median max VPD (kPa) | Threshold (σ) | Threshold (kPa) | Sites with a crossing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lowest | 52 | 2.90 | 0.25 | 1.00 | 52 |
| Q2 | 52 | 3.60 | 0.29 | 1.15 | 52 |
| Q3 | 52 | 4.37 | 0.16 | 1.33 | 52 |
| highest | 52 | 5.69 | 0.04 | 1.41 | 52 |

Every site crosses. From the lowest to the highest quartile the VPD range grows by
96 percent and the threshold by 41 percent, so the threshold is neither fixed nor
proportional to the range.

### Forest type comparison

The intervals in Figure 4 are prediction bands of the aggregated curve. Script 49 fits
one threshold per site and compares the distributions: Kruskal-Wallis H = 12.17,
p = 0.007; after Holm correction only ENF against DBF and DBF against MF differ. The
range of forest type medians is 0.19σ, the widest within-type interquartile range 0.52σ.

### Regional subsets and record length

Scripts 83 and 84 recompute the threshold with Europe, North America or both removed,
and under minimum record lengths of 3, 5 and 10 years, from the median of the per-site
thresholds. The same tests on the aggregated curve are rows of Table 1 (script 47), which
is the estimator the manuscript reports.

## ERA5 climate normals {#era5-climate-normals}

Script 17 gives each site one 1991 to 2020 mean annual temperature and precipitation
from the ERA5 fields in the FLUXNET files, the Copernicus CDS or Google Earth Engine.
Temperature and precipitation come from the same source, chosen on precipitation: below
2000 mm per year FLUXNET is used where available; above that, Copernicus replaces it
only when it is lower by more than 300 mm; a Copernicus value of zero is treated as a
failed download and Earth Engine is compared instead. Sites without FLUXNET ERA5 fall
back to Copernicus, then Earth Engine. Every decision is logged next to the output.
